citations.quote:
Let $Y$ be a closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold. A pointed genus-$g$ Heegaard diagram for $Y$ consists of an embedded splitting $Y=U_\alpha\cup_\Sigma U_\beta$, where $\Sigma=\partial U_\alpha$ is a closed oriented genus-$g$ surface and each $U$ is a handlebody, meaning a regular neighborhood of a finite connected graph; ordered systems $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_g)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_g)$ of pairwise disjoint smooth simple closed curves bounding specified disjoint proper compression disks in the respective handlebodies, each disk system cutting its handlebody into one ball; and one point $z$ off the curves. Opposite-system curves meet transversely in finitely many points. This is closed-manifold data; it includes neither a knot nor a second marked point.

Write $q:\Sigma^g\to\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)=\Sigma^g/S_g$ for the permutation quotient. The product tori are the images
$$T_\alpha=q(\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_g),\qquad T_\beta=q(\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_g).$$
The group $S_g$ acts on the ambient product, rather than on a fixed ordered product of distinct attaching circles. A generator is an intersection $x\in T_\alpha\cap T_\beta$; equivalently it selects one intersection point on each curve of each system. There are finitely many generators. For $g=0$ the symmetric product and both empty products are one point, with the empty generator.

A Whitney class $\phi\in\pi_2(x,y)$ is a relative homotopy class of maps of a closed disk with two marked boundary points into the symmetric product, taking its two boundary arcs into $T_\alpha,T_\beta$ and its marked points to $x,y$. Its domain is the integral two-chain of complementary regions; its coefficient at an interior point $p$ is the intersection multiplicity $n_p(\phi)$ with $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{g-1}(\Sigma)$. In particular $n_z(\phi)$ is the basepoint coefficient. A periodic domain is an integral region two-chain whose boundary is an integral sum of full attaching circles. The domain of a class $\psi\in\pi_2(x,x)$ is periodic. Such a class is normalized when $n_z(\psi)=0$. Write $\mu(\phi)$ for the real Fredholm index of the disk linearization, before quotienting longitudinal translation; well-definedness and its topological index formula are properties to be proved in the analytic and index theory.

For a periodic domain P, cap its full attaching-circle boundary with the specified compression disks, using the boundary multiplicities and orientations, to obtain the integral class $H(P)\in H_2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. A Spin-c structure $\mathfrak s$ is a lift of the oriented tangent frame bundle through $\operatorname{Spin}^c(3)\to SO(3)$; $c_1(\mathfrak s)$ is the first Chern class of its determinant line, with determinant character $[s,u]\mapsto u^2$. **Weak admissibility in the specified Spin-c sector $\mathfrak s$** means that EVERY nonzero integral periodic domain P with $n_z(P)=0$ and $\langle c_1(\mathfrak s),H(P)\rangle=0$ has both positive and negative region coefficients. This condition is imposed even when the sector has no diagram generators. It is a condition on domains and the intended sector, not only on periodic classes based at existing generators.

The ordinary sector module $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H,\mathfrak s)$ uses generators with Morse Spin-c label $\mathfrak s_z(x)=\mathfrak s$. The label is defined by compatible handle Morse data: replace the gradient in disjoint tubes around the generator's index-one/index-two trajectories and the basepoint's index-zero/index-three trajectory by nonsingular fields, and take the Spin-c lift of their oriented perpendicular planes. Its actual construction, independence properties and periodic-index formula are obligations of the Spin-c and index theory. In particular the equality between the index of a REALIZED normalized periodic class based at x and the Chern evaluation in $\mathfrak s_z(x)$ is not assumed as its own proof. A realized-generator test alone is not substituted for the stated domain condition.

An **admissible diagram for the full single-diagram hat module** satisfies this sector condition for EVERY Spin-c structure on Y, including the sectors with no generators. The full module below uses all generators and hence all intended sectors; an empty sector contributes a zero summand but is not omitted from the admissibility test. Equivalently this full-diagram condition is global weak admissibility: every nonzero periodic domain with $n_z=0$ has both signs. The equivalence uses the actual zero-Chern Spin-c sector constructed from complete Heegaard data in Complete Heegaard data have a zero-Chern Spin-c sector; it is not inferred from a generator existing in that sector. For a SINGLE specified sector, ordinary weak admissibility remains the stated Chern-kernel condition and need not imply global weakness. No assertion of the full group from a diagram tested only at its represented sectors is made.

For $g>0$ choose a complex structure $j$ and positive area form on $\Sigma$. Analytic data include a smooth path $J_t$ on the symmetric product, constant on actual neighborhoods of $t=0,1$. On a fixed neighborhood of the diagonal and the point-divisors for a chosen interior point of every complementary region, including $z$, it agrees with the integrable structure $\operatorname{Sym}^g(j)$; away from that neighborhood it is tame for the form descended from the product surface area form. The path is chosen in a sufficiently small nearly symmetric class. Product-integrable normal forms near the finitely many transverse generators may be included among its specified auxiliary choices. Existence of such choices and of the regular perturbations needed below remains a mathematical obligation. A holomorphic strip is an actual smooth finite-Dirichlet-energy map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)$ satisfying
$$u_s+J_t(u)u_t=0,\qquad u(s,0)\in T_\alpha,\quad u(s,1)\in T_\beta,$$
with uniform generator limits at both longitudinal ends. The space in class $\phi$ is $\mathcal M_J(\phi)$, and translation in $s$ acts on it. Regular means that its actual linearized operator is surjective at the solutions being counted. Local multiplicity positivity, Fredholmness, the class index and compactness are results to be proved, not choices of which maps to count.

The hat diagram-level module $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H;\mathbb F_2)$ is free over $\mathbb F_2$ on the generators. For regular data for which the displayed quotient sets are finite and, for each $x$, only finitely many nonempty pairs $(y,\phi)$ occur, its candidate count operator is
$$\widehat\partial x=\sum_y\ \sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(x,y)\\\mu(\phi)=1,\ n_z(\phi)=0}}\#_2\bigl(\mathcal M_J(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)y.$$
Here $\#_2$ is parity of an actual finite zero-dimensional quotient. For $g=0$ the operator is zero on the empty generator. That the required regular finite counts exist, that $\widehat\partial^2=0$, and that its homology is invariant under changing pointed admissible diagrams and auxiliary choices are separate analytic and move theorems. Once these hold, the common homology is denoted $\widehat{HF}(Y;\mathbb F_2)$. No filtered chain-homotopy invariant, integral orientations or absolute grading is asserted by this definition.

Comparisons of embedded diagrams permit orientation-preserving isomorphisms carrying $Y$, its two handlebodies, their oriented surface, the attaching systems and $z$ to the specified counterparts, equivalently compatible collared extensions of the surface map. Curve-factor reordering gives the corresponding product identification. Analytic data are transported by the induced symmetric-product map, including $j$, the area form, protected neighborhoods and $J_t$. The intended count identification is the actual pushforward of generators and disk classes with these transported data; its compatibility with the operator requires proof. An ambient isotopy is not assumed to act as the identity. Comparison of independently chosen perturbations likewise requires the continuation theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. Give a complete oriented Heegaard splitting $Y=U_\alpha\cup_\Sigma U_\beta$ of a closed connected smooth three-manifold, with actual disjoint compression disks cutting each handlebody into a ball. Then $TY$ has a Spin structure, constructed by finite handle and boundary-lift operations. Its induced Spin-c structure has trivial determinant line and hence first Chern class zero. In particular its Chern class evaluates to zero on every capped periodic domain, whether or not that sector has a generator in the given diagram.

Consequently the following two full-diagram conditions are equivalent: every nonzero normalized integral periodic domain has both signs; and for EVERY Spin-c structure $\mathfrak s$ on Y, including those with no diagram generators, every such domain with $\langle c_1(\mathfrak s),H(P)\rangle=0$ has both signs. This equivalence does not identify either condition with a test only at existing generators. For ONE specified sector, ordinary weak admissibility remains a separate condition.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix finitely many labelled attaching-circle families on a closed oriented surface with positive area form, finitely many protected points off all circles, and one witness point in every complementary region. Circles within a family are disjoint. Circles in different families are transverse, so their labelled pair intersections are finite; common points of three or more families are initially permitted.

Arbitrarily small smooth Hamiltonian isotopies of the individual families, supported away from all the protected and witness points, give pairwise transverse representatives with NO point on three curves from different families. Their pair intersections are canonically followed through the small isotopies, without birth or death. When the corresponding product tori have common POSITIVE rank $m>0$, no point belongs to three DISTINCT torus labels. At rank zero the empty product tori all equal the point of $\operatorname{Sym}^0\Sigma$; no exclusion of their triple intersection is claimed, and their source-dependent target transport is the identity. The complete disk-cut and based-link data can be transported by the family isotopies; no topology of the underlying handlebodies is changed.

Full-curve periodic-domain lattices and their sublattices generated by pairwise periodic domains transport bijectively by the swept annuli. All coefficients at the original witness and protected points are unchanged. Consequently any strict weak or strong admissibility criterion witnessed by these coefficients is preserved, when its indexing and linear evaluation are transported under this lattice map. Identification of that evaluation with a geometric Spin-c or Fredholm quantity is a separate topological assertion, not part of this lemma.

For an actual boundary-marked polygon source, the relative map spaces with fixed corresponding corner labels are homeomorphic by an actual smooth source-dependent target isotopy. It is the identity near protected incidence divisors and the diagonal and is fixed in the longitudinal coordinate on each far end. This induces bijections on literal continuous relative homotopy classes, without quotienting by a fundamental-group action. No symmetric power of a nonholomorphic surface map is used as a global smooth target map. For smooth fixed-end reference maps the transported actual Fredholm index is unchanged. These are class and admissibility transports, not an equality of holomorphic counts or an isotopy-invariance theorem.

Assume countable choice. Let $\Sigma$ be an oriented genus-$h$ surface, let $k\ge1$ and $m=h+k-1$, and give $q\ge3$ balanced attaching systems $\boldsymbol\eta^0,\ldots,\boldsymbol\eta^{q-1}$ of $m$ circles. Supply their disjoint compression disks in oriented handlebodies $U_i$, their compatible Morse functions with $k$ index-zero and $m$ index-one critical points, and $k$ distinct points $\mathbf w$ with one in each cut component of every system. Distinct systems meet transversely and finitely. Use the usual product tori in $\operatorname{Sym}^m\Sigma$. Let $W$ be the oriented polygon cobordism obtained from the polygon times $\Sigma$ by attaching $e_i\times U_i$ along $e_i\times\Sigma$, with rounded corners. A realized Whitney polygon is a continuous disk map with these successive torus edges and specified corner generators; no holomorphic representative is assumed.

The finite Morse construction below assigns such a class $u$ a Spin-c structure $\mathfrak s_{\mathbf w}(u)$ on $W$, restricting to the specified Morse labels of its corners. If $u,v$ have the same corners, their domain difference $P=D(u)-D(v)$ has boundary an integral sum of full attaching circles. Capping those circles with the supplied disks along polygon legs gives a class $H(P)\in H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$. With the common source/surface orientations, their Spin-c difference is
$$\mathfrak s_{\mathbf w}(u)-\mathfrak s_{\mathbf w}(v)=j\operatorname{PD}_W H(P),$$
where $j:H^2(W,\partial W;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(W;\mathbb Z)$. The sign is fixed by the positive index-one/index-two gradient modification having determinant degree $+2$ on a positive transverse disk.

In particular, if the two Spin-c structures and every $w$-multiplicity agree, then $P$ is a sum of actual doubly-periodic domains for the adjacent Heegaard pairs, each with all $w$-multiplicities zero. For a triangle these are the $\alpha\beta$, $\beta\gamma$ and $\alpha\gamma$ pairs. Their capped classes need not be zero individually. Fixed all $w,z$ multiplicities imply this hypothesis without any extra normalization convention.

The construction is compatible with gluing polygons along a common Heegaard boundary. Compatible Spin-c structures on the pieces have the usual extension orbit under the image of $H^1$ of that common boundary in $H^2$ of the glued cobordism; no unique extension is asserted. Along an actual continuous class-preserving family and its actual neck-smoothing, the assigned total Spin-c structure is constant, and the glued pieces recover that total extension, not an arbitrarily chosen member of the orbit. Point-divisor multiplicity vectors at every supplied $w,z$ mark add under these actual gluings. These assertions do not supply an analytic compactification or a gluing existence theorem. For supplied small attaching-curve isotopies away from the marks, transport the compatible Morse data in the actual handlebody collars and supply a continuous transport of the polygon maps. On the unchanged cobordism this carries their Spin-c labels and capped periodic classes, including torsion information. If one witness point in every old region misses the swept curves, all coefficients at those witnesses are unchanged. Hence strict strong admissibility, and the corresponding sector or global weak witness conditions, pass to the transported lattice. No existence of the continuous polygon-map transport is inferred from the mere isotopy of its boundary curves.

The statement does not identify all literal Whitney classes with their domains, divide genus-two classes by a sphere action, assert finiteness of classes with one domain, or supply any analytic count or Maslov-index formula. The point target $m=0$ has only the constant map and the domain conclusion is zero.

Assume countable choice and the actual finite balanced polygon data, a Spin-c structure $\mathfrak s$ on $W$, and one realized reference polygon $u_0$. Let $L$ be the lattice of formal integral periodic region chains $Q$ with $j\operatorname{PD}H(Q)=0$, and let $G\subset L$ impose zero multiplicity at every $w_l$. On $G$ put $\ell(P)=\langle c_1(\mathfrak s),H(P)\rangle/2$. The values of $\ell$ are integers. Assume the strict strong-admissibility condition
$$0\ne P\in G,\quad\ell(P)=N\ge0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\max_R P(R)>N.$$
Then the relative-index functional
$$\nu(Q)=\langle c_1(\mathfrak s),H(Q)\rangle+2\sum_l n_{w_l}(Q)$$
is strictly positive on every nonzero nonnegative direction in $L$. The nonnegative domains of actual same-corner, same-Spin-c polygons have a finite lower relative-index bound. For every integer $K$, only finitely many such nonnegative integral domains have relative index at most $K$. These statements concern domains, not the number of literal homotopy classes or holomorphic maps with one domain. They apply to actual Fredholm indices when the fixed-cap relative-index identification has been supplied.

For a boundary-pair sector the same conclusions hold with $L$ the FULL pair-periodic lattice, $G$ its all-mark-zero sublattice, and the Chern evaluation taken on its capped class in $Y$. Thus every nonempty fixed-end strip sector has a lower actual index bound $L_0$ and finitely many nonnegative domains of indices in $[L_0,K]$. For fixed attaching curves, marks and labels these bounds and finite sets are independent of the Cauchy–Riemann coefficients, auxiliary family parameters and source conformal parameters satisfying the same index conventions; they depend only on the finite domain lattice and Chern functional. No uniformity under an unspecified change of attaching curves is asserted.

There is also a weaker fixed-index statement. If every nonzero $P\in G$ with $\ell(P)=0$ has both signs, then at a fixed entire mark vector and any fixed finite set of relative indices there are only finitely many nonnegative domains in the fixed Spin-c sector. For supplied actual strip classes the pair version also holds under the separate weaker condition testing mixed signs only on REALIZED normalized index-zero periodic classes. Ordinary weakness for a specified Spin-c sector instead tests ALL formal normalized periodic domains with Chern evaluation zero, even when that sector has no generators; whenever an actual generator is supplied, the actual periodic index formula shows that ordinary specified-sector weakness implies this weaker realized-class condition. This proves a finite-domain statement only for supplied actual classes; it neither establishes invariance under moves nor supplies a generator in an intended sector whose generator set is empty. It does not give an unrestricted lower index bound. Any separately supplied uniform positive area bound also bounds every nonnegative component domain and hence its index, by its finite region coefficients.

There is a separate all-Spin-c zero-mark conclusion. If every nonzero formal periodic domain with all $w$ multiplicities zero has both positive and negative coefficients, then for fixed corners and fixed zero $w$ multiplicities there are only finitely many nonnegative domains, without fixing a Spin-c structure or an index. This global multi-periodic hypothesis is not inferred from strong admissibility for one Spin-c structure or from pairwise weak admissibility. No existence or winding construction of either type of diagram is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix a finite ordered list of distinct attaching systems with pairwise transverse product tori in $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m\Sigma$, $m\ge1$, and no triple intersection. Suppose every nonzero full-curve multi-periodic domain vanishing at the nonempty finite basepoint set $Z$ has both signs. Suppose also that each component of the complement of any one attaching system contains a basepoint. Fix a finite maximum arity $N$. Common compatible protected geometry with already supplied exact product-angle generator charts may be retained; their planes are $\mathbb R^m$ and $\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$ for arbitrary fixed $0<\theta_j<\pi$. Then there is a choice of common nearly symmetric target geometry and coherent source-dependent polygon structures for every ordered sub-list with at most $N$ inputs, having the following properties.

All structures fix whole common neighborhoods of the diagonal, every chosen region divisor and the basepoint divisors, and whole neighborhoods of the boundary tori and generator charts. They have genuine time-constant endpoint collars on each autonomous strip end. Every nonconstant zero-$Z$ end strip is regular, at every actual index. Every nonconstant zero-$Z$ polygon, with its conformal parameters included, is regular at every actual index. There are no constant stable polygons. On each finite-tree conformal face the limiting structures are precisely the already chosen structures on its vertices; their comparisons on retained cores and after every fixed number of neck derivatives are exponentially small. The uniform neck bounds and autonomous translated-neck limits required for the actual polygon compactness and gluing theorems hold.

When a compatible common protected tensor and an admissible coherent reference system have been supplied, the choices can be made arbitrarily close to that system in any prescribed finite collection of smooth coefficient norms on its compactified-family charts; the prescribed protected tensor and its actual corner angles remain unchanged. In particular a supplied integrable circular model is a legitimate reference. No count-preservation claim follows merely from this closeness.

The same relative construction gives generic smooth one-parameter coherent families between two such regular coherent choices with the same end paths and protected geometry. The parameter is included in the universal dimension, fixed endpoints are retained, and no regularity of every intermediate slice is asserted. This is a construction of analytic choices. It does not yet assert finite counts or an independence theorem for the resulting operations, and it does not replace sector admissibility by the stated stronger global hypothesis.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the coherent all-index regular data of the named supplier on a finite globally weak triple-free pointed multidiagram of rank $m\ge1$, with a basepoint in every one-system cut component. Fix any finite maximum arity. Label a polygon with $d$ incoming corners by $x_i\in L_{i-1}\cap L_i$, $1\le i\le d$, and output $y\in L_0\cap L_d$. Its positive boundary-edge order is $L_0,L_d,L_{d-1},\ldots,L_1$. Thus at an incoming corner the boundary traversal is $L_i\to L_{i-1}$; the incoming strip has $t=0$ on $L_{i-1}$ and $t=1$ on $L_i$. All counts are over $\mathbb F_2$ and impose zero multiplicity at every basepoint.

For $d\ge2$ the actual polygon count dimension is $\mu+d-2$; there is no triangle translation quotient. Its zero-dimensional total moduli are finite across ALL literal realized classes. Its one-dimensional total moduli compactify to compact one-manifolds whose boundaries are exactly the rigid polygon–polygon conformal splittings and rigid strip–polygon external breakings. Every such pair with matching generator has its actual exhaustive collar. No sphere, one-torus disk, constant polygon or additional escape stratum occurs. The same assertions hold after restricting to any actual class, using its actual concatenation rule.

Let $m_1$ count unparametrized index-one strips and, for $d\ge2$, let $m_d$ count polygons of fixed-map index $2-d$ with their $d-2$ conformal parameters. These finite maps satisfy the actual A-infinity identities
$$\sum_{r+s=d+1}\ \sum_{j=0}^{r-1}m_r(x_1,\ldots,x_j,m_s(x_{j+1},\ldots,x_{j+s}),x_{j+s+1},\ldots,x_d)=0.$$
Here $m_1$ on an output is included, and all label-compatible intermediate generators are summed. In particular the triangle map is a chain map and the quadrilateral count is its actual associativity homotopy.

For a generic coherent one-parameter triangle family with the same regular end strips, the universal index-minus-one moduli are finite; the universal index-zero moduli have compact one-dimensional boundary consisting of parameter endpoints and strip–triangle breakings. Their count gives the chain homotopy between the endpoint triangle maps. For rank $m=0$, the same count conclusions hold directly with the unique constant triangle counted once, zero differential, and all higher rigid operations zero. The source conformal boundary gives the same identities; no free strip-translation quotient is assigned to the constant point map.

This assertion concerns the supplied analytic choices, and does not assert a top-generator cycle, a Heegaard-move inverse, a Spin-c extension classification or filling identification.

Assume Countable Choice. Supply finite balanced polygon Morse data of rank $m=h+k-1\ge1$, with common $w,z$ marks, and no triple intersection of the product tori. Fix a Spin-c structure on the polygon cobordism and use the STRICT all-$w$ normalized strong admissibility condition of the named geometric lattice theorem. Use the same condition for its relevant boundary-pair sectors. The boundary systems have their actual complete $k$-ball cuts, and nearly symmetric geometry has exact constant product-angle generator charts. No $S^3$ or torsion restriction on the intermediate three-manifolds is made.

In the smooth topology, the genuine constant-collar end paths having no nonconstant strip of index at most zero and regularity for every actual index-one strip in the relevant sectors form an open dense subset of the allowed protected end paths. With these paths, compatible coherent source-dependent polygon perturbations can be chosen generically, relative to their faces and any regular parameter endpoints. Their count-dimension-zero total sets are finite, and their count-dimension-one spaces compactify to actual compact one-manifolds. All nonnegative $w,z$ degrees are retained. These conclusions hold for the fixed total Spin-c label, across all its literal realized classes; they also hold for fixed degree vectors or fixed actual classes. The boundary consists exactly of the label-compatible rigid polygon–polygon faces and strip–polygon breakings, with additive marked vectors and actual exhaustive gluing collars. No sphere or one-torus disk bubble occurs in these polygon dimensions. This includes $k=1$.

For triangles the fixed count index is $\mu$, so rigid counts have $\mu=0$ and the chain-map boundary has $\mu=1$. In a generic one-parameter triangle family with fixed regular end data the universal count index is $\mu+1$: the index-minus-one universal counts are finite, and universal index-zero spaces have the parameter endpoints and strip–triangle boundaries. Thus the finite actual counts satisfy the weighted triangle chain-map equation and its auxiliary-data chain homotopy over $\mathbb F_2$. They may be specialized to the two-color ring by sending every $w$ variable to $U$ and every $z$ variable to $V$. No top-generator cycle, handle-map inverse, arbitrary diagram invariance or absolute grading is part of this assertion.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix a globally weakly admissible complete pointed Heegaard diagram of ANY closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold, one integrable surface background $j$, area form and protected small Cayley coefficient family with common exact product generator charts. Let $J^0,J^1$ be two genuine time-collar paths with the same background endpoint structures, each regular at EVERY nonconstant zero-basepoint strip. Their actual index-one counts define the finite hat complexes $C^0,C^1$.

For a compact-transition source-dependent choice $K$ from $J^0$ to $J^1$ regular at every zero-basepoint solution, count its actual index-zero solutions WITHOUT translation quotient to obtain $\Phi_K:C^0\to C^1$. Then:

1. $d^1\Phi_K=\Phi_Kd^0$.
2. Two such compact-transition choices $K_0,K_1$ are joined by an ACTUAL regular relative parameter family. Its finite zero-basepoint index-minus-one solutions define a finite map $H$ with $\Phi_{K_1}+\Phi_{K_0}=d^1H+Hd^0$.
3. Continuation matrices compose up to this actual chain homotopy; their identity choice is the constant longitudinal path, whose matrix is the identity. Reversing the endpoints gives a continuation map which is a chain-homotopy inverse.

The one-dimensional moduli used for the first two identities have actual compactifications as compact topological one-manifolds with exactly the corresponding endpoint and broken boundary sets, with the actual exhaustive collars. Consequently all paths in this fixed-background protected family satisfying the stated regularity have chain-homotopy equivalent chosen hat complexes.

This compares AUXILIARY PATHS on the same globally weak diagram and the same integrable surface background. It does not compare different $j$, every merely sector-admissible diagram, attaching-circle moves, integral orientations, absolute gradings, Spin-c decompositions or plus/infinity/cobordism packages. No polygon counts are asserted. Genus zero gives the identity of the one-generator zero complex.

Assume Countable Choice. Put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m\Sigma$ for a closed connected Riemann surface, and fix finitely many product tori $L_j$ from systems of pairwise disjoint attaching curves. Let $a\in\Sigma$ lie off all these curves. The actual point-divisor bundle of $E_a=\{a\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}\Sigma$, with its canonical section on the boundary, defines integer degrees $n_a$ for disks and spheres, including contained spheres. It also defines an integer for every smooth strip between two transverse specified tori, with simultaneous product generator charts and uniform ends at their intersections: truncate and cap its ends inside sufficiently small generator charts avoiding $E_a$. The integer is independent of the sufficiently remote cuts and these local caps, and agrees with proper holomorphic intersection multiplicity whenever the latter is defined.

In the actual bounded-energy compactness conclusions of the bordered-source bubble-tree theorem, when the fixed source is a disk, or of the bubbled transverse-strip breaking theorem, these degrees satisfy, for all sufficiently large sequence indices,
$$n_a(u_n)=\sum_{\text{base or strip levels }v}n_a(v)+\sum_{\text{bubble components }w}n_a(w).$$
The hypotheses of those compactness theorems, including their common exact transverse generator charts for strips, are retained. No avoidance of $E_a$ by interior nodes or sphere bubbles is required. The formula holds simultaneously for any fixed finite set of such points.

In particular suppose the strip sequence satisfies that transverse-strip compactness theorem and the compact-bubble domain-energy lemma, with common diagonal and region-divisor neighborhoods and uniformly bounded geometric constants. Let $z_1,\ldots,z_k$ be marked points off all attaching curves, with $J_{n,t}$ and its limit equal to the standard symmetric-product structure near their divisors. Require that each connected component of the complement of each individual boundary curve system contains at least one of these marked points. If $n_{z_i}(u_n)=0$ for every $i,n$, its limit has no nonconstant sphere or disk bubbles. In fact no bubble vertices remain after discarding redundant constant vertices, and every retained strip level is nonconstant and has $n_{z_i}=0$ for every $i$. Thus that actual compactness theorem reduces to finite breaking of unbubbled zero-marked strips, with its smooth local convergence and full energy and neck-collapse conclusions. This does not assert regularity of same-generator index-two strips, a Maslov/domain-index identity, low-index stratum dimensions, or gluing.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the actual polygon map charts and nearly symmetric target geometry of the two named suppliers, with a fixed finite list of boundary labels and corners. Work over a finite-dimensional smooth open source/conformal/auxiliary parameter space $B$ of dimension $d$, with all neck lengths finite. Let $K_{b,z}$ be a smooth nearly symmetric coefficient family, equal to the specified transverse end structures near corner images, with uniform coefficient bounds on compact parameter subsets. Choose disjoint closed protected target neighborhoods $D,N$, with $D$ containing the diagonal and all chosen incidence divisors and $N$ a neighborhood of all the boundary tori and corner charts. The family is integrable on a neighborhood of $D$ and is tame elsewhere. Perturbations below fix neighborhoods of BOTH $D$ and $N$.

There is an explicitly constructed separable real Hilbert perturbation ball whose coefficient map is smooth into every fixed smooth compact-source norm, decays with every derivative faster than any exponential on each strip end, and has dense tangent fields on each compact subset of $B\times S\times(X\setminus(D\cup N))$. At EVERY actual nonconstant solution its universal Cauchy–Riemann derivative is onto on the actual $H^3_\delta\to H^2_\delta$ realizations. Consequently a residual set in this ball gives regular universal nonconstant polygon moduli of dimension $\mu+d$. In particular the spaces of negative such dimension are empty. When $d=0$ these are fixed-data regularity assertions; when $d=1$ slice counts are taken at regular parameter values, while the parameter is included in the universal dimension.

The construction can be restricted to an arbitrary open parameter region by multiplying its bumps by smooth parameter cutoffs, with universal surjectivity wherever those cutoffs are positive. It retains the chosen end limits and exact coefficients near every corner image; it does not claim that an infinite sum of source bumps is globally equal to the end data outside one common compact source subset. Nor does it claim regularity of constant polygons, compactness, coherent extension over nodal conformal faces, or count identities. Constant polygons must be treated or excluded separately in the application.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix a closed complex surface curve $(\Sigma,j)$ with positive area form $\eta$, and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m\Sigma$, $m>0$. Let $L_0,\ldots,L_{n-1}$ be finitely many attaching product tori. Choose one interior point $q_R$ of each region cut out by all their attaching curves, and include any prescribed basepoints in this finite protected list. Let $D$ be a closed neighborhood of the repeated-point locus and these incidence divisors, disjoint from all the product tori. Write $\omega$ for the descended product area form off the repeated-point locus.

Let $u$ be a smooth finite-energy polygon on an actual punctured half-plane source with these successive boundary labels and uniform transverse corner limits. Suppose its source-dependent structure $J_z$ equals $\operatorname{Sym}^m(j)$ on one fixed open neighborhood of $D$ and tames $\omega$ elsewhere, with uniform taming and coefficient bounds. Then every region and marked multiplicity is a nonnegative integer and
$$E(u)\le C\sum_R n_R(u)\operatorname{Area}_\eta(R).$$
The constant depends on the target metrics, protected neighborhoods and uniform structure bounds, but not on the conformal positions of the punctures. The same bound applies to a family with these common bounds. Domains are locally constant under boundary-preserving fixed-corner homotopies.

Choose a closed neighborhood $N$ of the union of the tori disjoint from $D$. Every nonconstant such polygon has a source-interior point where $du\ne0$ and $u$ lies outside $D\cup N$. Thus a nonconstant polygon has a nonempty open set of nonzero derivatives in a free target region even when perturbations fix a whole neighborhood of all boundary tori. The statement does not assert that a constant polygon can be regularized by changing $J$.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix finitely many compact attaching product tori with pairwise transverse finite intersections, common exact product generator charts, fixed full boundary tensors on each torus and fixed nearly symmetric protected target geometry. Consider actual polygons on the sources in the finite-tree conformal charts. Suppose their source-dependent coefficient families have uniform smooth bounds on vertex compact subsets and unit neck windows. On every neck and external end they equal the common product structure near each relevant generator. Along any sequence receding from both vertex cores on a neck, all translated coefficient derivatives on compact windows converge to the specified autonomous end path. On an external end assume the same end convergence. Coefficient convergence is uniform in the target. On each labelled physical boundary its full tensor on that torus is the fixed boundary tensor, independently of the longitudinal source coordinate. Families assembled by the explicit vertex sewings with rapidly convergent end coefficients have these properties.

Every sequence of actual smooth polygons with fixed external corner labels and uniformly bounded energy has a subsequence with a finite stable limit: polygon components on a finite conformal source tree; finite chains of autonomous strips on its internal edges and external ends; and finite trees of nonconstant spheres and one-torus boundary disks at concentration points, with stable constant components where needed. Convergence is smooth on compact subsets away from the finite nodal points after the actual conformal rescalings and strip translations. All bubble and strip necks have vanishing lost energy and vanishing image diameter; attached values agree. Total energy is the sum of the component energies. For the fixed protected incidence points their nonnegative degrees add exactly across these components. No regularity, dimension or index assumption is used.

In particular, if every prescribed basepoint degree is zero and each attaching-system complement component contains one such basepoint, all sphere and one-torus disk bubbles are constant and are removed from the stable description. Only polygon vertices and strip chains remain. The theorem does not classify low-dimensional ends, prove transversality or construct gluing collars.

The exact end charts may have arbitrary constant product angles $0<\theta_j<\pi$. All transverse Fourier and cutoff estimates below use the positive finite minimum of $\theta_j$ and $\pi-\theta_j$; no orthogonal crossing normalization is required.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix actual nearly symmetric polygon data with common exact transverse generator charts and smooth source/target coefficient bounds. In each matching chart the boundary planes are $\mathbb R^m$ and $\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$, with $0<\theta_j<\pi$; set $g$ to the positive finite minimum of $\theta_j$ and $\pi-\theta_j$ over the matching ends. Decay exponents and any weights are chosen below $g$, not below an assumed right angle. Consider either two regular polygon components joined at a transverse matching corner, or one regular polygon component and one regular nonconstant strip joined at an external corner. Include the components' actual conformal parameters in their derivatives, and quotient the strip component by its actual translation. Suppose the component count dimensions are zero. Fix representatives, using a smooth compact-source phase for the strip.

Suppose the actual coefficient data on the sewn sources agree asymptotically with the component data in their finite-tree neck charts as follows: on each fixed component core their difference and all required derivatives are $O(e^{-cT})$; they have uniform smooth bounds on the neck; and they are EXACTLY the common product structure wherever a map value is in the matching generator chart. The same estimates hold after differentiating in $T$. For polygon–polygon sewing $T$ is its actual new conformal neck parameter. For strip–polygon sewing it is the strip core's longitudinal position relative to the polygon core; the polygon has no translation quotient.

For all large $T$ there is a regular corrected polygon, and modulo the stated component phases these polygons form an injective half-open collar. Their index and count dimension are the actual sums: the glued count dimension is one. Every sequence converging to this unbubbled two-component breaking, with the actual strong compact convergence and no-neck convergence, is eventually in this collar. Kernel matching and bounded right inverses are proved below; they are not extra hypotheses. The collar is smooth for finite $T$ in the solution charts, and is a topological half-interval after adding its broken endpoint. No differentiability in a prescribed compactifying parameter at the endpoint is asserted.

More generally, for any fixed finite unbubbled tree of regular polygon and nonconstant strip components, the construction gives actual local product charts with the component solution coordinates and one positive gluing coordinate for each node. Their dimension is the sum of the component count dimensions plus the number of nodes. These charts exhaust every sequence with that component limit and strong compact and no-neck convergence. The constants may depend on that fixed component tree and small component charts. The assertion supplies neither a uniform inverse across unrelated components nor regularity of an arbitrary limiting component.

Assume countable choice. Let $X$ be compact with a fixed smooth metric, $J_t$ a smooth family of almost complex structures, and $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ a smooth nonconstant solution of
$$u_s+J_t(u)u_t=0$$
with finite Dirichlet energy and uniform limits $x_-,x_+$ as $s\to-\infty,+\infty$. Let $K\subset X$ be any finite set containing these limits. Then the set
$$\mathcal R(u)=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R\times(0,1):u_s(s,t)\ne0,\ u(s,t)\notin K,\ u(s',t)=u(s,t)\Rightarrow s'=s\}$$
is open and dense in the interior strip.

In particular this applies to actual finite-energy strips with compact totally real boundary submanifolds of finite transverse intersection and fixed longitudinally independent boundary structures: their uniform ends exist by the transverse-end-convergence theorem. The conclusion concerns injectivity at a fixed time coordinate. It does not assert global injectivity of $u$ or ensure that a point of $\mathcal R(u)$ lies outside a prescribed closed region of allowed almost-complex perturbations.

derivations.claim: The admissibility inputs are actual domain bounds, not a formal assumption that the desired moduli are compact. For a full single-diagram hat module, [F1] supplies a zero-Chern sector independently of whether it has generators; the required all-sector test therefore tests EVERY normalized periodic domain and gives the global weak pair condition. For several systems the multiperiodic condition in the Statement is imposed on the actual chosen auxiliary multidiagram; pairwise conditions alone are not substituted for it. Its nonnegative zero-mark domains are finite before any index or regularity choice, as proved in [F3]. For the ordinary weak specified-sector branch, fix the finitely many required corner tuples, arities and count dimensions zero and one. If a source has $d$ inputs and $p$ allowed family parameters, its fixed-map index is its count dimension minus $d-2+p$; the finite strata of a compact parameter family therefore require only a finite list of actual indices. Strips and anchored profiles have their stated respective index shifts. At zero entire mark vector [F2] supplies finitely many nonnegative domains for each such fixed Spin-c family and index list, independently of coefficients. Include the actual continuous concatenations representing the total classes of the required boundary identities: their total index is the same prescribed finite list by actual cap additivity, their marks are zero, and their total Spin-c extensions are the specified ones. Thus their domains belong to those same affine slices, not to a hypothetical finite class list. If a slice is nonempty choose one actual reference in it; there are only finitely many slices, so this uses finite choice. Their union is finite. The domain-energy estimate of [F6] supplies a uniform energy bound $E_0$ before the coefficient choices, on a small family with uniformly bounded geometric constants. Enlarge the finite list for the finitely many separated compositions and relative homotopies required, and choose a strict energy budget $E>E_0$. In the strict branch [F2] separately supplies its stronger finite upper-index domains and lower strip index. No lower index bound is claimed for ordinary weak data.

Treat rank zero by [F3]'s direct model. Its map operator is the zero operator between zero spaces and is onto of index zero. A triangle has one matching constant map, no conformal parameter and no continuous automorphism. A higher stable polygon has its actual positive source dimension and no rigid contribution. The four-marked source is an interval whose two ends are the two constant triangle products, and its parity is zero over the coefficient field. A matching one-parameter triangle family is its parameter interval; other assigned labels or nonzero marked vectors give empty sets. There are no nonconstant strips or bubbles. This proves the point-target count identities without excluding an allowed genus-zero input.

For positive rank apply [F2], protecting the basepoints and a witness in each old region. Pair generators persist without births, and the swept-annulus integral lattice transport preserves old sign witnesses. The actual collar extensions carry the compression disks, capped classes and Spin-c lifts. Consequently the prescribed admissibility and labels hold on the chosen representative. No constant stable polygon can occur: its at least three distinct boundary labels would give a common point of three product tori. This curve choice is explicit and necessary; the coefficient variation at a constant map is zero because its derivative is zero, so a J-only genericity assertion on the original arbitrary fixed triple would be false. Nothing in this step asserts count invariance under the curve change.

Reconstruct the reverse divisor bound needed for ordinary weak components. For each chosen region point $a$, its actual divisor bundle has the canonical nonzero section $\sigma$ on a neighborhood of the compact union of the fixed boundary tori. If a permitted compact family of boundary tracks is used, take its whole union and require the chosen divisor to avoid it; here the analytic coefficient families keep the chosen attaching curves fixed. Choose $U_1\Subset U_0$ about that union, disjoint from the divisor, and use the flat connection in frame $\sigma$ on $U_0$. Cover the remaining compact target by finitely many line frames with flat local connections; a finite smooth partition, whose $U_0$ coefficient is one on $U_1$, patches them to a connection $\nabla$. In a frame write $\nabla e=Ae$. The transformation $A'=A+g^{-1}dg$ makes $F=dA$ a global smooth bounded two-form, zero on $U_1$. In a pulled-back disk frame write $\sigma=f e$ along the boundary. There $A=-f^{-1}df$, so Stokes gives $\int u^*F=-2\pi i\operatorname{wind}f=-2\pi i n_a(u)$, with the actual relative degree convention in [F6]. For a finite-ended polygon or anchored strip truncate every end in its common exact generator chart inside $U_1$, multiply its coordinate map by a real cutoff and cap at the generator. Scalar multiplication preserves both product boundary planes, with arbitrary specified angles. All modified pieces and caps have $F=0$, so the same integral formula holds on the uncapped source, independently of those choices. Pointwise $|u^*F|\le C|du|^2/2$, hence $|n_a(u)|\le C_aE_g(u)$. This is not a reversal of energy bounded by domain area. Finitely many region points simultaneously bound EVERY component domain with energy at most $E$, regardless of its split Spin-c label. The same curvature estimate on omitted necks and the actual energy identity give integer degree additivity: core integrals converge, remaining integrals tend to zero, and convergence of the resulting integers is eventual equality. This applies at nodes on divisors and to contained compact bubbles, without a zero-set avoidance assumption.

Choose genuine end paths good on the energy budget without a lower-index assumption. Start in any prescribed smooth neighborhood of the compatible reference paths. Use the actual source-free, time-slice-injective universal argument in [F6]. A nonconstant strip has a free site outside the protected divisor and torus neighborhoods, since an entire image in the latter misses EVERY region divisor and has zero energy. A time-slice injective point and adjoint unique continuation localize a time-only variation there. The explicit countable Hilbert smoothing series with flat time-end jets and ACω Sard give auxiliary paths onto at EVERY nonconstant zero-mark strip, over ALL actual indices and component sectors. This uses no global finite-domain assertion. Cut the auxiliary paths to their fixed endpoint values in shrinking time collars. Flatness gives smooth convergence. If nononto zero-mark strips of energy at most $E$ existed for infinitely many late cuts, [F6]'s actual compactness would give a finite auxiliary limiting chain. Degree additivity and positivity exclude every zero-mark sphere and one-torus disk, because every one-system cut component contains a basepoint. All retained nonconstant levels are onto, with the same exact transverse end operators. Patch their actual right inverses and whole transverse neck inverses by squared cutoffs. Fixed-core operator differences tend to zero; each neck commutator is $O(1/T)$ and exact-generator tail errors tend to zero. Taking component-core transitions long, then the subsequence late, makes the finite sum of errors smaller than one; Neumann correction gives a right inverse, a contradiction. No bound on the unknown indices of these strips was used. If the entire limit is constant, energy tends to zero; step2.1 makes every integer region degree eventually zero, and the domain-energy estimate forces the original strip to be constant. Its exact transverse operator is invertible and cannot be a counterexample. Thus a late genuine-collar path is onto at every zero-mark solution of energy at most $E$. The same compactness argument proves openness on this budget; starting the auxiliary choice in any specified neighborhood proves density. Choose these paths for the finitely many end pairs.

In the global branch use [F3]'s all-index end choices and coherent polygon data. Its finite face induction preserves any supplied compatible protected tensor and every supplied product angle, and its source-local Hilbert variations are positive at every finite neck length and flat at the conformal faces. Thus genericity is genuine even at large finite necks. In the strict branch use [F4]. Its finite lower-index band and unconditional bubble index budget first exclude every nonconstant strip of index at most zero; its index-one regularity then suffices for every limiting strip which can occur in a low-dimensional polygon. In the ordinary weak branch use step3.1 on the chosen budget and repeat the source-local Hilbert coefficient construction: neither universal surjectivity nor the finite coherent face induction uses global weakness or a lower index bound. It makes nonconstant polygon vertices regular at every actual index. Their relevant limiting strip levels inherit energy at most $E_0<E$ by the actual energy identity, so those strips are onto and have index at least one from their nonzero translation vector. No regularity outside that energy budget is presumed. All three branches fix genuine time-constant endpoint collars and include every allowed source parameter in the actual operator.

For a compact auxiliary parameter manifold $B$ with finitely many boundary charts, construct regularity jointly at its conformal faces; do not assign its dimension separately to different vertices. The autonomous end paths are fixed. On a prescribed planar face with vertices $v$, use the configuration space $B\times\prod_v\mathcal B_v$ and the direct-sum section $(\bar\partial_{b,v}u_v)_v$, with each strip phase treated as in [F6]. Its derivative is $((D_v\xi_v+C_v\dot b)_v)$, with ONE shared vector $\dot b\in T_bB$. At stable vertices the ordered boundary-label sublists of a finite ordered polygon face are distinct. Thus their source-local coefficient bumps are independent even at a common target value; these are variations of different ordered coefficient systems. At each nonconstant polygon vertex the universal bump argument of [F6] kills its obstruction, while every autonomous end level within the energy budget is already onto by step3.1. Hence the joint universal derivative is onto. Its parameter projection has Fredholm index $\sum_v a_v+\dim B$, where $a_v$ is its fixed-parameter component count index, including its conformal parameters and the actual autonomous strip phase. Apply the countable Hilbert Sard construction simultaneously over integer-index strata, corner tuples and finite face trees up to the fixed maximum arity. There are countably many such map charts and only finitely many label lists and tree types. Coefficient bumps are flat at conformal faces but positive in every vertex's interior; the finite arity induction therefore retains lower prescribed face data and achieves these joint conditions. On boundary faces of $B$ retain already jointly regular compatible data and induct over their finite face strata; source/parameter bumps vanish there, and interior parameter regularity is obtained as in the actual relative construction. This produces joint regularity, not regularity of every individual fixed-parameter polygon slice at a critical parameter.

The joint regular zero chart also supplies actual common-parameter gluing when an individual polygon vertex is not onto at fixed $b$. Take one bounded right inverse $Q$ of $((\xi_v),\dot b)\mapsto(D_v\xi_v+C_v\dot b)_v$ on the finite limiting tree; its finite-dimensional parameter vector is shared, not copied. For a forcing on the glued source, use the squared cutoffs to split it into the vector of component forcings, apply this single $Q$, and cut and glue the resulting section components while retaining its ONE output $\dot b$. On component cores the resulting composition is the identity by the defining joint equation for $Q$. Generator-chart parameter derivatives vanish, since protected geometry is fixed, and the remaining parameter coefficients decay along the ends by the rapid coefficient bounds. Consequently the commutator and mismatch estimate is exactly the finite sum $C/T_e+o(1)$ of [F6], with the extra parameter term bounded by its vanishing tail coefficient times the common finite energy norm. Neumann correction gives the augmented glued right inverse. The two cutoff maps on kernels are inverse for long necks by the same error estimate, now retaining $\dot b$ once; thus the local zero-chart dimensions and injectivity are the actual ones. Apply the proved Newton correction in the map/source charts with that shared parameter and the neck variables. Its derivative estimates, and the converse closeness of an actual convergent sequence to its pregluing, are unchanged because the parameter ranges in a compact finite-dimensional chart. This gives an exhaustive collar modeled on the joint component zero space times its neck coordinates. In particular a zero-dimensional joint face is one broken configuration with a fixed common parameter, even when its two polygon components are not separately rigid universal spaces.

Use [F6] with step1.1's uniform total energy bound in the ordinary weak branch, or the proved applications [F3] and [F4] in the other branches. Degrees add at every actual region divisor. A zero-basepoint sphere has its constant surface coefficient zero; a one-torus disk has constant coefficient on each one-system cut component, each of which contains a basepoint. Their domain-area inequalities force zero energy, so no nonconstant such bubble remains, including when it is entirely contained in a protected divisor or the diagonal. Constant compact ghosts are deleted only when unstable; no stable polygon vertex is deleted by that convention. The latter cannot be constant here by step1.3. At fixed coefficients the total count dimension is the sum of the regular vertex count dimensions plus the number $q$ of nodes, with one longitudinal phase removed only for an actual autonomous nonconstant strip. In a common-parameter family it is instead the JOINT component count dimension in step5.1 plus $q$, by actual cap and source-tree additivity. That joint dimension is nonnegative by regularity, even when an individual vertex has negative fixed-parameter index. Consequently dimension zero is unbroken; a non-interior dimension-one limit has exactly one node and a rigid joint two-component configuration. With no auxiliary parameter these are the two ordinary rigid components. This rules out every extra multi-level, multi-conformal or bubble escape in the dimensions used by the asserted identities.

Finiteness and collars are topological conclusions of the proved analytic construction, not consequences of a merely formal dimension count. An unbroken convergent sequence converges in the global map chart by the exact end cutoff inverse. A rigid total set is discrete and sequentially compact across all its literal classes, hence finite under ACω by selecting ordered finite distinct tuples and flattening them. Each matching fixed-data pair, or matching common-parameter joint configuration, has its actual nonlinear chart and unique exhaustive half-interval collar by step6.1. All components inherit the total energy bound, independently of their possible split Spin-c labels; step2.1 bounds their domains without reversing the area inequality. The rigid joint boundary sets themselves are finite by the same compactness and joint dimension argument: a further splitting would have another node and negative joint face dimension. Thus no separate assumption of finitely many component classes or separately rigid parameterized vertices is required. Distinct positive-energy cores and strip phases separate distinct collar endpoints. The resulting Hausdorff second-countable sequentially compact one-manifold is compact; its finite interval boundary has even parity. The actual class, total Spin-c label and degrees are locally constant in map charts and carried by explicit neck sewing, so imposing any such label selects the corresponding open-and-closed part and does not assume a class/domain bijection.

For a polygon with $d$ inputs the count dimension is the actual fixed-map index plus $d-2$ conformal parameters; a triangle has no such parameter and no translation quotient. The rigid operations are therefore the index-one strip differential and the polygon counts of index $2-d$. Enumerating the actual one-node ends in step8.1 gives precisely the finite A-infinity sum, including the output differential and every input differential. This proves differential square-zero, the triangle chain-map equation and the quadrilateral composition homotopy. For a compact auxiliary family use the actual joint construction in steps5.1–6.1. Its broken boundaries are the zero-dimensional common-parameter fiber configurations, not in general products of individually rigid parameterized polygon spaces; its prescribed parameter boundary strata are included as well. The parameter is counted once. Fixed-data A-infinity products remain precisely the ordinary products already enumerated. In particular universal index-minus-one triangles are rigid and universal index-zero triangles have their endpoint and strip-breaking boundaries. Counts of those boundaries give the asserted homotopy identities. Zero-basepoint boundary-degeneration terms are zero by step7.1, hence no omitted contribution remains to cancel. The analytic theorem supplies these identities for the actual admissible diagrams and inputs; computing named top cycles, constructing surgery multi-diagrams, identifying filling homology and proving move inverses require their own proofs and have not been assumed here.

For continuation retain the compact-transition source profile as part of the equation. The global branch is [F5]. For ordinary weak specified-sector data reconstruct its analytic proof on step1.1's energy budget rather than apply its global-admissibility Statement. The actual anchored compactness has one unshifted central component and autonomous escaping levels; zero marks exclude bubbles by step2.1's degree argument. Universal source-dependent bumps make the central augmented operator onto on all index strata. Fixed ends only need regularity within the energy budget, supplied in step3.1; constants in a protected generator chart have the exact invertible transverse operator. For a relative parameter family fix its regular endpoints and use parameter-interior source bumps; endpoint zero charts are already regular. The flat time and rapid source smoothing series can be cut to genuine time collars and compact source transitions: a nononto sequence of energy at most $E$ has an anchored auxiliary limit with onto augmented central operator and onto autonomous end levels. The squared-cutoff inverse retains the one central parameter output and has error $O(1/T)+o(1)$; its parameter forcing is zero on generator necks and uniformly vanishing on escaping cores. Neumann correction contradicts nononto-ness. An entirely constant limit is handled by step2.1 and the zero-domain energy estimate, and its constant operator is already invertible. Thus a late genuine profile or family is regular at every relevant energy-bounded zero. The central rigid continuation operator has index zero with NO translation quotient. Its exact constants count the identity. This proves the required continuation chain maps, composition and inverse homotopies within the specified sector without importing a global index bound. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $C$ and $D$ be finite integer-filtered chain complexes over $\mathbb F_2$, each with total homology isomorphic to $\mathbb F_2$. A filtered chain homotopy equivalence consists of filtration-preserving chain maps $f:C\to D$ and $g:D\to C$ such that $gf$ and $fg$ are chain homotopic to the respective identity maps by homotopies that preserve every filtration level. Then $\tau(C)=\tau(D)$.

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot in $S^3$, let $F$ be a compact connected oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $\mathcal H_0,\mathcal H_1$ be admissible multipointed Heegaard diagrams for $K$. For $i=0,1$, the diagram $\mathcal H_i$ has a closed genus-$h_i$ Heegaard surface and $m_i=h_i+k_i-1$ curves in each attaching system, with $k_i$ ordered $w$-points and $k_i$ ordered $z$-points; each component of either attaching-system complement contains one point of each type, and the connecting arcs represent $K$. A curve isotopy is an isotopy of one attaching curve through embedded curves in its attaching system, disjoint from the other attaching curves and all marked points. A handleslide replaces one attaching curve by its band sum with another curve in the same attaching system, along an embedded arc disjoint from the other attaching curves and the marked points. A Heegaard stabilization forms connected sum with the genus-one splitting of $S^3$ in a disk disjoint from all curves, marked points, and knot arcs; it raises the genus by one and leaves $k$ fixed. A basepoint-pair (index-zero/three) stabilization keeps the genus fixed and adds one curve to each system and one $w,z$ pair along the represented knot. Its inverse removes the following elementary configuration, after relabeling the cyclic pairs: curves $\alpha_0,\beta_0$ bound disks $A_0,B_0$ on the surface, are disjoint from every opposite-system curve except each other, and intersect transversely in two points; $A_0\cap B_0$ is a bigon containing just $w_0$, while $A_0\setminus B_0$ contains just $z_0$ and $B_0\setminus A_0$ contains the next $z$-point along the cyclic pairing. Remove $\alpha_0,\beta_0,w_0,z_0$ and concatenate the adjacent trivial knot arcs. The surviving marked points stay fixed. Thus the move inserts a pair along an existing knot arc rather than adjoining an isolated marked component in an empty disk. Both descriptions include the simultaneous boundary-parallel arc systems and require the stated one-$w$, one-$z$ condition in each attaching complement. Destabilizations are the respective inverse moves. Comparisons may apply the orientation-preserving diagram isomorphisms of the pointed-data definition, carrying the ordered marked points, attaching systems and simultaneous boundary-parallel arcs, before or after the listed geometric moves. Their complex identifications are induced by pushforward of generators, disk classes and almost complex data, rather than by assuming an isotopy acts as the identity. Comparisons also allow the fixed-splitting arc normalizations in that definition before or after the listed moves, retaining the simultaneous bridge witnesses and all ordered marks. They leave the surface attaching and analytic data fixed, so their identification of the actual count operators is the identity; they do not assert a diffeomorphism of a tangential and transverse surface-knot pair. With these identifications, any two such diagrams are related by a finite sequence of the listed moves through admissible multipointed diagrams, preserving the represented oriented knot.

For a diagram with $j$ basepoint pairs, regard its full filtered minus complex as a complex over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by restriction of scalars along $U\mapsto U_i$ for any one chosen basepoint variable. The resulting complexes of $\mathcal H_0$ and $\mathcal H_1$ are filtered chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb F_2[U]$, preserving relative Maslov grading and Alexander filtration, even when the diagrams have different numbers of basepoint pairs. The choice of the single variable action does not affect this type. Restriction retains the independent variables in the chain module; it is different from quotienting by $U_1=\cdots=U_j$. The latter ordinary quotient is the fully collapsed complex and has filtered chain homotopy type $CFK^-(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(j-1)}$, where $V$ has zero differential and bidegrees $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$. Equivalently, a basepoint stabilization before quotienting is modeled by the cone of $U_{j+1}+U_i$ on the polynomial extension of the old complex; after the simultaneous quotient this is a zero-map cone and contributes the displayed extra factor.

For an admissible doubly-pointed diagram $\mathcal H_1$ for $(K,F)$, define $\widehat{HFK}(K)$ to be the homology of the Alexander-associated-graded complex obtained from its full filtered minus complex by quotienting by its sole variable $U$. For a generator $\mathbf x$ use the Alexander grading
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the relative $\operatorname{Spin}^c$ structure assigned by the pointed Heegaard construction from the gradient trajectories through $\mathbf x$ and the chosen basepoint pair, and $\widehat F$ is obtained by removing a tubular neighborhood of $K$ from $F$ and capping the resulting longitude with the meridian disk of the solid torus attached so that this longitude bounds it (zero-framed surgery). The vector-field representative is extended across small balls around the critical points, and its first Chern class is the Chern class of the orthogonal oriented plane field. Use the absolute Maslov normalization in which the unique generator of $\widehat{HF}(S^3)$ has degree zero.

For a diagram $\mathcal H$ with $j$ basepoint pairs, let $\widetilde C(\mathcal H)$ be the Alexander-associated-graded complex over $\mathbb F_2$ obtained from its full filtered minus complex by setting every $U_i=0$; its differential therefore counts only classes with all $n_{w_i}=n_{z_i}=0$. Its homology is $\widehat{HFK}(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(j-1)}$, where $V=\mathbb F_2\langle v_0,v_1\rangle$ has bidegrees $(M,A)(v_0)=(0,0)$ and $(M,A)(v_1)=(-1,-1)$.

Let $G$ and $G'$ be one-component grid diagrams related by one of the following local moves. A cyclic permutation changes the planar cut of the toroidal grid by moving the first row or column to the last. A row commutation exchanges consecutive rows whose closed horizontal marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested; a column commutation uses the same condition on vertical marking intervals. A stabilization replaces a marked cell by a two-by-two block with the original marking type in two opposite cells and the other type in a third cell, leaves the fourth cell empty, and inserts one row and one column, relocating the old companion markings so each new row and column has one mark of each type. Any of the four empty corners is allowed, and destabilization is the inverse move. Regard each full filtered minus complex returned by the grid-complex algorithm as a complex over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by letting $U$ act as one chosen marking variable $U_i$, retaining the other independent variables. The resulting complexes are filtered chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb F_2[U]$, with equivalences preserving the Maslov grading and Alexander filtration. For each move, finite grid-domain counts give filtered chain maps in both directions and filtered chain homotopies from both composites to the identity. For a stabilization, its multivariable target is first compared with the cone of $U_{n+1}+U_i$ on the polynomial extension of the original complex. After instead taking the simultaneous ordinary quotient $U_1=\cdots=U_n=U$, a stabilization contributes a zero-map cone, equivalently an extra zero-differential factor $V$; those fully collapsed complexes are compared with this factor retained. Under commutation the tilde homologies are isomorphic; under a stabilization from grid number $n$ to $n+1$, the tilde homology changes by tensoring with the two-dimensional bigraded vector space $V$ with one generator in bidegree $(0,0)$ and one in bidegree $(-1,-1)$.

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $F$ be a compact connected oriented surface embedded in $S^3$ with boundary $K$ and minimum possible genus; write $g(K)=\operatorname{genus}(F)$. Let $G$ be any toroidal grid diagram for $K$ with grid number $n$. Let $C^-_{\mathrm{grid}}(G)$ be the full filtered minus complex produced by the grid-complex algorithm, and let $C^-_U(G)$ denote this same complex regarded over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by letting $U$ act as one chosen $U_i$, with the other variables retained independently. For an admissible $2n$-pointed Heegaard diagram $\mathcal H$ compatible with $(K,F)$, define $C^-_U(\mathcal H)$ by the same restriction to a single variable action. Write $CFK^-(K)$ for the full filtered complex of an admissible doubly-pointed diagram. The ordinary fully collapsed quotient, obtained instead by setting all $U_i=U$, has type $CFK^-(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)}$; the restriction of scalars $C^-_U$ has type $CFK^-(K)$.

For the absolute Alexander normalization, let $\mathcal H_1$ be an admissible doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram for $(K,F)$. For a generator $\mathbf x$ of $\mathcal H_1$, set
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the relative $\operatorname{Spin}^c$ structure assigned to this generator by the pointed Heegaard construction: it is the homology class of the nowhere-vanishing vector field obtained from the gradient trajectories through $\mathbf x$ and the chosen basepoint pair, after extending the field across small balls around the critical points. Its first Chern class is that of the oriented plane field orthogonal to this vector field. The surface $\widehat F$ is obtained by removing a tubular neighborhood $N(K)$ from $F$ and capping the resulting longitude with the meridian disk of the solid torus attached in zero-framed surgery on $K$. Let $\widehat{HFK}(K)$ be the homology of the Alexander-associated-graded complex obtained from the doubly-pointed complex $C^-_U(\mathcal H_1)$ by quotienting by its sole variable $U$, with this $A_F$ normalization.

Then $C^-_U(G)$ and $C^-_U(\mathcal H)$ are filtered chain homotopy equivalent, preserving relative Maslov grading and the $A_F$ filtration, and their Alexander-associated-graded minus complexes are chain homotopy equivalent. For any two grids of $K$, the resulting normalized filtered complexes are filtered chain homotopy equivalent. If $\widetilde{GH}(G)$ denotes the homology of the tilde grid complex over $\mathbb F_2$, then
$$\widetilde{GH}(G)\cong\widehat{HFK}(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)},$$
where $V$ is the two-dimensional bigraded vector space with one generator in bidegree $(0,0)$ and one in bidegree $(-1,-1)$.

Assume countable choice. Let $G_0,G_1$ be finite planar grid diagrams, with vertical segments over horizontal segments and orientation from $O$ to $X$ in rows and $X$ to $O$ in columns, representing the same oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere. A cyclic permutation moves the first row or column to the last position. A row commutation exchanges adjacent rows when the closed intervals between their respective $O$- and $X$-mark abscissae are disjoint or one lies in the interior of the other; a column commutation is defined by the same condition on the intervals between marking heights. A stabilization chooses a marked cell and temporarily removes its marking together with the other markings in its row and column. It splits that row and column into two, places the three removed markings, and adds one new $O$-mark and one new $X$-mark so that every row and column again has one of each. In the four-cell subdivision of the chosen cell, exactly three cells are marked: the chosen marking type appears twice, the other type once, and any one corner may be the empty cell; the two other markings removed from the original row and column are placed outside this block in the new row and column. A destabilization is the inverse operation. Then a finite sequence of cyclic permutations, commutations, stabilizations, and destabilizations carries $G_0$ to $G_1$.

derivations.claim: Apply [L1] to the two analytic doubly pointed diagrams in the Statement. Its maps and inverse homotopies are finite polynomial identities preserving their Seifert-normalized Alexander filtration. Specialize those identities at U=0; no flatness assertion about homology is required. The resulting actual finite hat models are filtered chain homotopy equivalent and carry the nonzero total generators to each other. Therefore [F1] gives equality of their thresholds. This proves the analytic-diagram comparison in the first sentence.

Fix a grid $G$ with $n$ marking pairs and choose one marking variable $U_i$. Use the actual normalized grid-to-analytic comparison in [L3], together with the pointed-move comparison in [L1], to convert its full filtered minus complex to the finite singly pointed model for $(K,F)$. In this comparison first restrict scalars along $U\mapsto U_i$ and retain the other $U_j$ as independent module variables. The supplied chain maps and inverse homotopies preserve the Alexander filtration and the Seifert-normalized origin. Specializing these actual identities at the chosen $U=0$ gives the corresponding filtered equivalence to the singly pointed hat endpoint. The restricted grid module can still have infinite rank over $\mathbb F_2$ after this specialization, so it is not itself an input to the finite-complex definition of $\tau$; the grid value in the Statement is the threshold on the finite normalized singly pointed endpoint obtained by this conversion.

The separate simultaneous ordinary collapse sets all marking variables equal before taking the one-variable quotient. By [L3] and [L1] its filtered type is the singly pointed minus model tensored with $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$, with each $V$ carrying bidegrees $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$. After quotienting the remaining variable by zero, this collapsed model has the extra $V$ homology factors and is not the finite complex with one-dimensional total homology required in the definition of $\tau$. Those factors are accounted for by the actual basepoint-pair cone and retraction comparison in [L1, L3]: use the retained-variable equivalence to the singly pointed model when defining the grid's value, and do not apply $\tau$ to the unreduced simultaneous-collapse complex. Thus no extra filtration shift from the $V$ factors is included in the claimed value.

For any two grid presentations, [L3] supplies this conversion for each grid to a normalized singly pointed model. Compare those finite endpoints by the actual pointed-move equivalence [L1], specialize its maps and filtered inverse homotopies at $U=0$, and apply [F1]. This gives the same threshold as in step 1.1. The grid-move and grid-isotopy suppliers [L2, L4] describe additional combinatorial comparisons; they do not replace the filtered grid-to-analytic conversion or alter the variable-collapse distinction above.

citations.quote:
Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere. Let $F$ be a compact connected oriented Seifert surface with boundary $K$, and let $\mathcal H=(\Sigma,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,w,z)$ be an admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagram representing $(K,F)$. The associated one-pointed hat chain complex $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is the finite-dimensional chain complex over $\mathbb F_2$ obtained from the minus complex by setting its basepoint variable to zero; its differential counts index-one disks with zero multiplicity at $w$. Assume for this specified data that the differential is nonincreasing in the Alexander filtration, that the absolute Alexander formula below takes integer values, and that $H(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))\cong\mathbb F_2$. Give a generator $\mathbf x$ its absolute Alexander filtration
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the homology class of the nowhere-vanishing vector field assigned to $\mathbf x$ by the pointed Morse construction, with its prescribed boundary data near the two basepoints; $c_1$ is the first Chern class of the oriented plane field perpendicular to that vector field. To form the zero-framed surgery, remove a tubular neighborhood of $K$ and glue in a solid torus whose meridian is the longitude induced by $F$. The surface $\widehat F$ is obtained by deleting a boundary collar of $F$ and capping its longitude by the meridian disk of that solid torus. This is the standard integer normalization, with the one-generator diagram of the standard unknot at filtration zero. The subcomplex $F_s\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is spanned by generators of Alexander filtration at most $s$.

More generally, a finite integer-filtered chain complex is a finite-dimensional chain complex $C$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with subcomplexes $F_sC$ such that $F_sC=0$ for all sufficiently small integers $s$ and $F_sC=C$ for all sufficiently large integers $s$. If $H(C)\cong\mathbb F_2$, define
$$\tau(C):=\min\{s\in\mathbb Z:\operatorname{im}(H(F_sC)\longrightarrow H(C))\ne0\}.$$
For the fixed diagram and surface above, write $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)=\tau(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H),F_*\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))$. Once diagram and surface independence is proved, their common value is the knot invariant $\tau(K)$. Until that comparison is proved, $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)$ denotes only the value for the specified data.

derivations.claim: Put $t=\tau(C)$. By [F1], some class in $H(F_tC)$ maps to a nonzero class in $H(C)$. Since $f$ preserves filtration, its restriction sends $F_tC$ to $F_tD$.
